back: Buys goods and resells them unchanged (e.g. a grocery or hardware shop).
Converts raw materials into finished goods for sale (e.g. a bakery, a furniture workshop).
Sells skills or work, not goods (e.g. a salon, a driving school, a transport operator).
The owner is personally responsible for all business debts; private assets can be sold to pay creditors.
A shareholder can lose no more than the amount paid for the shares.
Easy to start; quick decisions; owner keeps all profit; personal service; privacy.
Unlimited liability; limited capital; long hours; may end if the owner dies or is ill; hard to expand.

front: How many partners does a partnership normally have?
back: Two to twenty. Profits and losses are shared in the agreed ratio (equally if there is no agreement).

front: Is a sole trader's business separate from its owner?
back: Not legally, but it is in the accounts (business entity), so personal spending is drawings.
